raw_response.overlap_rationale: Both full texts are accessible and represent two distinct review/synthesis articles produced under the same Himalayan Adaptation, Water and Resilience (HI-AWARE / CARIAA) research consortium and published in the same special issue of Water Policy, 22(S1) (2020), by completely different author teams (Vishal Singh and Anvita Pandey at CEDAR in Study A vs. Sreoshi Singh, S. M. Tanvir Hassan, Masooma Hassan, and Neha Bharti at ICIMOD/BCAS/PARC/TERI in Study B). Study A explicitly cites the online-first version of Study B (Singh et al., 2019). Neither paper reports a primary household or official survey sample; instead, both synthesize secondary municipal water statistics and published/grey literature across Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) cities. However, they exhibit partial overlap in their compiled city-level water demand-and-supply datasets and case-study narratives: 4 of the 8 cities tabulated in Study A Table 1 (Quetta, Shimla, Mussoorie, and Kathmandu) are also among the 13 cities tabulated in Study B Table 9, with identical or rounded-identical secondary MLD figures for Quetta (170 MLD demand, 106 MLD supply) and Mussoorie (14.4 vs. 14.5 MLD demand; 7.67 vs. 7.7 MLD supply), as well as the exact same 210 MLD shortage figure for Kathmandu Valley in the text (plus shared qualitative discussion of Pokhara, Almora, Leh, and Srinagar). At the same time, each paper covers substantial non-overlapping material: Study A extends to Afghanistan (Kabul), China (Xining), Bhutan (Thimphu, Phuentsholing), and Nainital and formulates 12 urban water governance/resilience recommendations (including groundwater bye-law enforcement against informal tanker markets), whereas Study B conducts a census-based demographic and urban-definition analysis (1981-2011) across Bangladesh, India, Nepal, and Pakistan and includes 9 cities not in Study A's table (Rangamati, Baramula, Darjeeling, Kohima, Tansen, Pokhara, Rawalpindi, Mansehra, and Karak). Consequently, there is partial underlying secondary-data overlap and a moderate risk of double-counting city-level MLD deficits and case observations for the shared HKH towns.
raw_response.study_a_sample_and_data: Narrative synthesis and secondary-data policy review of urban water resilience in the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) conducted under the HI-AWARE (CARIAA) consortium. No primary survey or fieldwork sample (N) is reported. Compiles secondary municipal water supply and demand data (in MLD) and major water issues in Table 1 for N = 8 cities across 6 countries: Kabul (Afghanistan), Quetta (Pakistan), Shimla, Mussoorie, and Nainital (India), Kathmandu (Nepal), Xining (China), and Thimphu (Bhutan), alongside narrative discussion of Pokhara, Baglung, Almora, Leh, Srinagar, Manali, Gangtok, Dharamshala, Dehradun, Haldwani, and Phuentsholing using published literature, government reports (e.g., NITI Aayog 2018), and media sources up to 2019.
raw_response.study_b_sample_and_data: Literature and national-census review of urbanisation definitions, migration/tourism drivers, water supply deficits, and household/government coping and adaptation strategies across the HKH regions of 4 countries (Bangladesh, India, Nepal, and Pakistan), conducted under the HI-AWARE (CARIAA) consortium. No primary survey sample (N) is collected. Analyzes secondary national census datasets—Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (2011), Census of India (2001, 2011), Nepal Central Bureau of Statistics (2001, 2011), and Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (1981, 1998)—and compiles secondary municipal water demand, supply, and deficit data (in MLD) in Table 9 for N = 13 urban centres: Rangamati (Bangladesh); Baramula, Shimla, Mussoorie, Darjeeling, and Kohima (India); Tansen, Kathmandu Valley (KUKL), and Pokhara (Nepal); and Quetta, Rawalpindi, Mansehra, and Karak (Pakistan).
